prime.problem: Packet delay is mostly time waiting in queues, and with no limit on senders there is no limit on the queue. So a timeout can only be a guess: too short and healthy nodes get declared dead, too long and failures sit unnoticed. Meanwhile, if every sender just sends as fast as it can, the queues overflow for everyone.
prime.fits: Builds on the unreliable-network card, which used 2d + r without saying where d comes from. This card derives a real worst-case d (QJUMP), shows its throughput price, and explains how TCP's AIMD keeps queues short when there is no bound.
expect: QJUMP's f: trade the bound for throughput
AIMD: +1 per RTT, halve on loss
why AIMD converges to fairness and AIAD doesn't
prime.goal: Compute a worst-case delay bound and the timeout it allows, explain what rate-limiting costs, and trace AIMD's sawtooth and why its halving makes flows converge to a fair share.

attend: Why is the worst case "all n hosts send to one destination at once", and why is the bound doubled for a mesochronous network?
What does QJUMP's f assume about how many hosts send at once, and what happens to the guarantee when that assumption fails?
Why does 2d + r need a real maximum d, and what do you use on the internet instead?
Why does AIMD keep the path only about 78% full on average in the 16-packet example?
Why does multiplicative decrease shrink the gap between two flows, while additive decrease never does?

must: Delay is queueing → queues are unbounded unless every sender is rate-limited → with rate limits, the worst case is all n hosts sending to one place: τ ≤ 2nP/R + ε (413.6 µs for 1,000 hosts) → the bound holds only because everyone obeys it

A hard bound caps each host at ~R/2n (5 Mb/s at f = 1) → QJUMP assumes only n/f senders at once → bigger f = more throughput, weaker guarantee → per-priority f lets latency-critical traffic keep the bound
Timeout = 2d + r → needs a real maximum one-way delay d → only a bounded network gives one → otherwise d is a percentile you choose and the timeout stays a guess

No bound → senders must slow themselves → AIMD: +1 packet per loss-free RTT, halve on loss → a sawtooth that keeps queues from growing forever (8 → 17 → 8, mean 12.5 of 16) → halving cuts the bigger flow by more, so flows converge to fair shares
elevated: Loss-based AIMD reacts only after a queue overflows → it keeps queues full and adds delay → data-centre traffic uses early signals instead (ECN/DCTCP marks, BBR's path model)
reference: QJUMP's example values (256 B packets, 10 Gb/s, ε = 1–4 µs)
802.1Q priority levels 0–7 and the ~35-cycle rate limiter
Wang & Ng's EC2 loss numbers (< 0.5%, episodes in > 10% of intervals)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw two chains: (1) rate limits → bounded queue → bound τ → timeout 2d + r, with the throughput price; (2) no bound → AIMD sawtooth → short queues and fairness. One number on each.
checklist: a bound needs every sender rate-limited: 413.6 µs for 1,000 hosts, 5 Mb/s each
f trades the guarantee for throughput
timeout 2d + r is a fact only with a real d
AIMD: +1 per RTT, ÷2 on loss, mean ≈ 78% of capacity here
multiplicative decrease is what makes flows fair

retrieve.q: Explain why a timeout is a guess on the internet but can be a fact on a QJUMP network.
answer: on the internet no one bounds the queues, so delay has no maximum
QJUMP rate-limits every host so the worst case is computable (τ ≤ 2nP/R + ε)
with a true d, silence past 2d + r really means failure (877.2 µs in the card's example)

retrieve.q: Walk through the AIMD trace from RTT 0 to the first drop and one full cycle after it: the window values, when the drop happens and why the cycle is 10 RTTs.
answer: cwnd starts at 1 and grows by 1 per RTT
then 8, 9, …, 17 again: 10 RTTs per cycle, drops at 16, 26, 36
mean window (8 + 17) / 2 = 12.5 = 78% of 16; 430 packets in 40 RTTs

retrieve.q: You set the image service's resize timeout to 2d + r = 540 ms. What happens if you cut it to 150 ms to "fail faster", and what if you raise it to 5 s?
answer: 150 ms is below r for many real resizes and below GC pauses: healthy workers are declared dead, their load moves, more time out (cascade)
5 s: real failures wait 5 s to be noticed, eating the p99 budget ten times over
the timeout must sit above the real d and r percentiles; crash signals handle the fast case

compare.q: AIMD slows a sender when the network's queue overflows; backpressure slows a caller when a server's queue is full. What is the same mechanism underneath, and what signal does each use?
answer: both keep a queue short by making the sender slow down
AIMD's signal is a lost packet (implicit); backpressure's is an explicit fast error or a blocked put
both need the sender to cooperate: rejected callers back off exponentially, TCP halves its window

compare.q: TCP halves its window on loss; the retries card doubles the wait between retries. Both are multiplicative responses to trouble. Why multiplicative in both cases, and what does jitter add that AIMD doesn't need?
answer: multiplicative response backs off fast enough to relieve an overloaded resource (the one thing additive can't do quickly)
for retries, many clients fail at the same instant, so they'd return together; jitter spreads them
TCP flows lose packets at different times already, so their sawtooths desynchronise without explicit jitter

predict.q: Double the path capacity: AIMD with a drop whenever cwnd > 32, starting at 1, for 40 RTTs. When is the first drop, how many drops happen in 40 RTTs, and what is the steady-cycle mean as a share of capacity? Commit, then run aimd(cap=32).
predict.answer: The first drop is at RTT 32 (cwnd 33 → 16), and it's the only one in 40 RTTs; 694 packets are sent. The steady cycle is 16, 17, …, 33: 18 RTTs, mean (16 + 33) / 2 = 24.5 = 76.6% of 32. Over 80 RTTs the drops land at 32, 50 and 68. A bigger pipe makes the sawtooth slower (18 RTTs per cycle instead of 10), which is why +1 per RTT is too timid for fast long-distance links.

apply.task: Use epoch_us and rate_per_host from code/delay-timeouts-congestion.py for a smaller cluster: n = 500 hosts, 256 B packets, 10 Gb/s, ε = 4 µs. Compute the mesochronous epoch at f = 1, the per-host rate, and the 2d + r timeout with r = 50 µs. Then compare with the card's 1,000-host numbers.
apply.done: You get an epoch of 208.8 µs (half of 413.6 µs), about 10 Mb/s per host (twice the card's 5), and a timeout of 2 × 208.8 + 50 = 467.6 µs, and you can say why halving n halves the epoch but doesn't touch ε.
apply.hint: 2 × 500 × 2,048 bits / 10<sup>10</sup> b/s = 204.8 µs, plus ε = 4 µs. The per-host rate is ≈ R / 2n = 10<sup>10</sup> / 1,000 = 10 Mb/s.
